paragraphs: Recommendation systems must often judge an item before much interaction history has accumulated around it. This is the item cold-start problem, and it becomes especially pressing when new items arrive continuously, as Tweets do. The paper addresses this setting with a meta-learning strategy designed to adapt recommendation models using an item's history.

The authors introduce two deep neural network architectures that implement this strategy in different ways. One learns a linear classifier whose weights depend on the item history. The other learns a neural network and adjusts its biases instead. Both make the item's history part of how the predictor itself is configured, giving the system a way to adapt its recommendations as information about an item becomes available.

The evaluation uses production data from Twitter. Both the matrix-factorization baseline and production Tweet recommendation models are outperformed by the proposed techniques, with significant gains reported over matrix factorization. These findings support the usefulness of the meta-learning approach in the continuously arriving-item setting examined by the paper.
neurips-2017-a-meta-learning-perspective.tldr: Two meta-learning architectures adapt predictors using item history and outperform matrix factorization and production models on Tweet recommendation data.

paragraphs: This paper studies a sequence whose underlying mean changes at a small number of locations. The statistical task is to estimate that mean and identify where changes occur. The authors analyze the fused lasso estimator in this one-dimensional setting, assuming that the mean vector has relatively few changepoints.

Their main result is a fast error rate that comes close to the minimax benchmark, the reference rate for the best achievable worst-case performance. The gap is only a factor of log log n. This gives a sharper account of how accurately the fused lasso can estimate the signal under the stated sparsity assumption. The proof centers on a new construction called a lower interpolant.

The authors also extend their results to misspecified models and exponential-family distributions. They explain how the estimation-error analysis bears on approximate changepoint screening: using an estimated signal to narrow down plausible change locations. The contribution therefore connects a near-benchmark estimation guarantee with the practical task of finding candidate changepoints.
neurips-2017-a-sharp-error-analysis-for-.tldr: Under sparse changepoints, the paper establishes a fused-lasso error rate within a log log n factor of the minimax rate.

paragraphs: Recognition and recall often produce different patterns of memory performance. This paper argues that several such differences can arise from an imbalance built into classic experiments: they contain more items to remember than retrieval cues. Its proposed account treats recall as retrieving items from a cue, while recognition retrieves associated cues from an item.

The authors test this account by changing the numbers of items and cues within a memory experiment. They observe a crossover within participants. Recognition works better when items outnumber cues, whereas recall works better when cues outnumber items. The direction of the advantage therefore changes with the structure of the experiment, as the theory predicts.

A computational model implements the account by using sampling to approximate an ideal Bayesian observer that records and retrieves co-occurrence frequencies between items and cues. It reproduces several recognition–recall dissociations previously used to support dual-process explanations of declarative memory. The findings show how a shared computational account can explain those patterns through differences in retrieval direction and experimental structure.
neurips-2017-a-simple-model-of-recogniti.tldr: A Bayesian sampling model explains several recognition–recall differences through the relative numbers of remembered items and retrieval cues.

paragraphs: Maximum a-posteriori inference asks for the most probable joint assignment in a graphical model. Large instances make efficient optimization increasingly important. This paper focuses on solvers that use dual decomposition and coordinate minimization, and asks whether their updates can run faster when several processors work at the same time.

The proposed approach performs message-passing updates asynchronously. Multiple processing units read and write shared memory without coordinating their updates with one another. This changes the execution of the solver: individual updates can proceed while other processors are also updating the shared state. The central technical question is how this concurrent execution affects convergence and when it provides a speed advantage.

The authors analyze convergence properties and identify settings in which speedups can be expected. Numerical evaluations on common computer vision tasks show significant improvements in speed. The result supports asynchronous parallel execution as a way to accelerate this class of inference solvers, with the analysis tying that benefit to particular settings.
neurips-2017-asynchronous-parallel-coord.tldr: Asynchronous shared-memory updates accelerate coordinate-minimization MAP solvers, with convergence analysis and significant speedups on computer vision tasks.

paragraphs: Parallel computations can be held back by a few slow workers, often called stragglers. This paper develops a technique inspired by error-correcting codes for linear inverse problems solved with particular iterative methods. Its goal is to improve the estimate available when a computational deadline arrives, even when workers have progressed at different speeds.

The method combines outputs from all workers, including the slow ones. Their partial contributions therefore help determine the final estimate. This design also makes accuracy degrade gradually when many workers are slow. The applications discussed include personalized PageRank and sampling on graphs, both presented as examples of relevant inverse problems.

The authors prove that their approach can reduce mean-squared error under a deadline constraint. In their analysis, the error ratio between replication-based and coded methods grows without bound as the deadline increases. Personalized PageRank experiments on real systems and social networks produce ratios as large as 10,000. These results demonstrate substantial gains within the iterative-computation setting studied.
neurips-2017-coded-distributed-computing.tldr: An error-correcting-code-inspired method uses all workers' outputs to improve deadline-limited inverse-problem estimates despite stragglers.

paragraphs: The paper studies continuous optimization problems with a diminishing-returns structure called DR-submodularity. These objectives can be non-convex, yet their structure permits useful algorithmic guarantees. The focus is maximizing non-monotone functions, where increasing a variable need not improve the objective, under general down-closed convex constraints.

The authors first establish geometric relationships between approximately stationary points and the global optimum. These relationships make local optimization information useful for obtaining global approximation guarantees. A two-phase algorithm achieves a one-quarter approximation and can use existing stationary-point methods as a subroutine. A second algorithm, a non-monotone variant of Frank–Wolfe, achieves a 1/e approximation with sublinear convergence.

These guarantees describe how much of the optimal objective value the algorithms can secure within the studied problem class. The paper also extends the approach to generalized DR-submodular functions and checks its theoretical findings on synthetic and real-world instances. Motivating applications include inference in determinantal point processes and probabilistic submodular models, connecting the optimization results to structured probabilistic reasoning.
neurips-2017-continuous-dr-submodular-ma.tldr: Geometric properties of continuous DR-submodular functions yield maximization algorithms with one-quarter and 1/e approximation guarantees.

paragraphs: Understanding how brain regions synchronize requires models that preserve relationships across recording locations and signal frequencies. This paper introduces Cross-Spectral Factor Analysis, or CSFA, for multisite low-frequency recordings such as local field potentials and EEGs. Disrupted synchronization in disorders including schizophrenia and depression motivates the need for interpretable descriptions of these networks.

CSFA decomposes recorded signals into factors with distinct spatial and spectral properties. A Gaussian-process formulation within a multiple-kernel-learning framework gives the factors this structure. The resulting lower-dimensional representation retains information relevant to neuroscientists while making its components interpretable in terms of patterns across locations and frequencies.

In the reported experiments, CSFA achieves similar performance to commonly used, less interpretable approaches when classifying mouse genotype and behavioral context. The authors also introduce a semi-supervised extension called discriminative CSFA. Together, the methods are presented as tools for understanding neural dynamics and helping design causal follow-up experiments; the classification results demonstrate usefulness alongside the interpretability of the representation.
neurips-2017-cross-spectral-factor-analy.tldr: CSFA extracts interpretable spatial-frequency factors from neural recordings while retaining competitive classification performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Learning to control a continuous system becomes harder when observations are substantially noisy. The controller must act using an imperfect view of the underlying state. This paper extends PILCO, a data-efficient reinforcement learning method, to account for that uncertainty during policy planning in a Gaussian partially observable setting.

PILCO evaluates policies through trajectories predicted by a learned dynamics model, but its original policies act on observed states. The proposed extension incorporates filtering and plans in belief space: a representation of uncertainty about the state. This makes the planning process consistent with the information available to a controller operating under partial observability.

The distinction matters because adding a filter after optimizing a policy leaves that optimization unaware of the filtering process. The authors report that integrating filtering into planning enables data-efficient learning under significant observation noise and outperforms such post-hoc approaches. Their test uses cartpole swing-up, a task involving nonlinear dynamics and nonlinear control, demonstrating the benefit in the continuous-control problem examined.
neurips-2017-data-efficient-reinforcemen.tldr: Integrating filtering into PILCO's policy planning improves data-efficient cartpole learning under significant observation noise.

paragraphs: Combining data sources can produce training examples for a new task, but the labels obtained this way may be unreliable. This paper addresses that problem with a meta-algorithm for learning from noisy labels. Its central idea separates the decision to perform an update from the procedure used to calculate that update.

This separation makes update timing an explicit part of the learning method. A training rule determines how parameters change, while a distinct decision determines when that rule should act. The authors describe the resulting approach as simple to implement and analyze some of its convergence properties, connecting the practical learning procedure with theoretical questions about its behavior.

For an empirical demonstration, the authors construct a gender-classification dataset by combining faces from Labeled Faces in the Wild with a text-based gender-labeling service. This combination produces noisy labels, providing a direct test of the proposed approach. They report state-of-the-art results in this demonstration, supporting the value of controlling when learning updates occur in the presence of label noise.
neurips-2017-decoupling-when-to-update-f.tldr: A simple meta-algorithm separates update timing from update computation to improve learning with noisy labels.

paragraphs: Deeper convolutional networks can learn stronger visual representations, but their larger parameter spaces also make training challenging. This paper proposes changing the basic convolution operation to learn angular representations on hyperspheres. The new operator, SphereConv, provides the foundation for a network architecture called SphereNet.

SphereNet combines SphereConv with a generalized angular softmax loss, aligning the training objective with the angular representation. The approach makes hyperspherical geometry part of both feature computation and supervision. The authors also introduce a learnable version of SphereConv, extending the fixed operator, and SphereNorm, which uses hyperspherical learning as a normalization method.

The paper reports that SphereNet learns discriminative representations while easing optimization and converging faster than conventional convolutional counterparts. Classification accuracy is comparable and sometimes better in the reported comparisons. Theoretical insights accompany experiments supporting these conclusions. Together, the results suggest that changing the geometry of representation learning can improve training behavior while preserving, and in some cases improving, classification quality.
neurips-2017-deep-hyperspherical-learnin.tldr: SphereNet learns angular representations on hyperspheres, with reported improvements in optimization and convergence alongside competitive classification accuracy.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging measures fluorescence that indirectly reflects neural activity, so recovering spike trains requires computational inference. Bayesian model inversion can address this problem, but repeated sampling is expensive, while maximum-a-posteriori optimization supplies a faster approximation. This paper trains a neural network to perform the inversion efficiently using a variational-autoencoder framework.

The approach amortizes inference by learning the computational work in advance. Its recognition network is trained to generate samples from the posterior over spike trains. After training, inference requires a single forward pass, avoiding a new iterative optimization or sampling procedure for each input. The framework can therefore represent uncertainty over possible spike trains while providing fast inference.

The authors show that the approach works with a range of nonlinear generative models and substantially improves computation time while maintaining competitive accuracy. They also demonstrate its flexibility with a probabilistic method for separating backpropagating action potentials from putative synaptic inputs in dendritic-spine imaging. This application extends the framework beyond extracting a single undifferentiated activity signal.
neurips-2017-fast-amortized-inference-of.tldr: A variational-autoencoder framework learns fast posterior inference for neural spike trains from calcium imaging, achieving competitive accuracy.

paragraphs: An underdetermined optimization problem leaves room for multiple solutions, making the solution selected by the learning procedure an important question. This paper studies that choice for a quadratic objective over a matrix. The matrix is represented through a factorization, and gradient descent operates on the factors.

The central conjecture is that this procedure converges to the minimum nuclear-norm solution when the step sizes are sufficiently small and initialization is sufficiently close to the origin. Nuclear norm measures the sum of a matrix's singular values. The factorization is full-dimensional, so the proposed preference concerns the behavior of optimization within that parameterization.

The authors provide both empirical and theoretical evidence for the conjecture. Its significance is a possible implicit regularization effect: the way a matrix is parameterized and optimized can favor a particular solution without explicitly adding that preference to the objective. The claim remains a conjecture supported by evidence, with small steps and near-origin initialization central to its stated form.
neurips-2017-implicit-regularization-in-.tldr: The paper supports a conjecture that small-step gradient descent on matrix factors, initialized near zero, selects a minimum nuclear-norm solution.

paragraphs: Graph embeddings turn nodes into compact numerical representations useful for prediction. Many existing methods require all nodes to be present during training, which makes unseen nodes difficult to handle naturally. This paper introduces GraphSAGE, a framework that learns how to generate embeddings from node features and local graph neighborhoods.

GraphSAGE samples a node's neighborhood and aggregates features from the sampled nodes. Training therefore produces a function that can be applied to new nodes, rather than only a collection of embeddings tied to the training graph. Feature information, such as text attributes, supplies inputs that the learned function can use when a previously unseen node appears.

The authors evaluate GraphSAGE on three inductive node-classification benchmarks and report improvements over strong baselines. Citation and Reddit data test classification of unseen nodes in evolving information graphs. A protein-interaction dataset tests transfer to entirely unseen graphs. These findings demonstrate both forms of generalization in the studied datasets: handling new nodes and generating useful representations in new graphs.
neurips-2017-inductive-representation-le.tldr: GraphSAGE learns to generate node embeddings by sampling and aggregating neighborhood features, enabling prediction on unseen nodes and graphs.

paragraphs: Textual grounding connects a description to a region in an image. Existing methods commonly choose among bounding boxes proposed by an earlier deep-network stage. That setup makes the final prediction depend on whether the proposal stage supplied a suitable region. This paper develops a unified framework that can efficiently search all possible bounding boxes.

Searching this larger space removes reliance on a successful initial proposal set and allows globally optimal prediction within the model's formulation. The paper also gives the learned parameters an interpretable role: they can serve as word embeddings that capture spatial relationships in images. The model thus links language with image structure in a way that can be inspected.

At submission, the method reportedly exceeded the then-current state of the art on Flickr 30k Entities and ReferItGame by 3.08% and 7.77%, respectively. These benchmark findings support the proposed search formulation's practical value. The contribution combines broader region search with parameters that help explain the spatial-image relationships learned from language.
neurips-2017-interpretable-and-globally-.tldr: A textual-grounding framework efficiently searches all bounding boxes and learns interpretable word representations, improving reported benchmark results.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning in an unknown, weakly communicating Markov decision process over an unlimited time horizon. The learner must choose actions while learning the environment's dynamics. The proposed algorithm, Thompson Sampling with Dynamic Episodes, uses uncertainty over model parameters to select a policy for each episode.

At the start of an episode, the algorithm samples a model from its posterior distribution and follows that model's optimal stationary policy. Episode duration is controlled by two stopping criteria. One limits how quickly episode lengths grow; the other ends an episode when the visit count for any state–action pair doubles. These rules determine when the learner resamples its model.

The authors establish a Bayesian expected-regret bound of order HS√(AT), up to logarithmic factors, where S and A count states and actions, T is elapsed time, and H bounds the span. This matches the best available bound reported for weakly communicating MDPs. Numerical results also show better performance than existing infinite-horizon algorithms in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2017-learning-unknown-markov-dec.tldr: Thompson sampling with dynamically ended episodes achieves a matching Bayesian regret bound for weakly communicating infinite-horizon MDPs.

paragraphs: A slate recommendation policy selects an ordered group of items based on context, as in search rankings or advertising. Evaluating a new policy using previously logged interactions requires estimating how that policy would have performed. This paper introduces a practical estimator for this task, drawing on techniques from combinatorial bandits.

The authors derive conditions under which the estimator is unbiased, meaning its average estimate matches the target performance. Those conditions are weaker than assumptions used by earlier slate-evaluation heuristics. Theory and experiments also show exponential reductions in required data relative to general unbiased estimators, making the structure of the slate problem central to the efficiency gain.

Experiments on real-world data find accurate estimates across several settings. The estimator also performs competitively when used inside a learning-to-rank task. When its unbiasedness conditions are violated, it still shows smaller bias than parametric alternatives in the reported experiments. That last finding is empirical robustness evidence, distinct from the conditional guarantee of unbiasedness.
neurips-2017-off-policy-evaluation-for-s.tldr: A slate-policy estimator uses logged data efficiently, with conditional unbiasedness guarantees and strong empirical accuracy.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain mapping starts with two datasets whose examples are not paired. The goal is to translate an example from one domain into its counterpart in the other. Previous approaches obtained convincing mappings by learning both translation directions together. This paper develops a method that learns only the desired forward mapping.

The method constrains the mapping to preserve distances between pairs of samples. This supplies a relationship that can be maintained across domains even without matched examples. The authors also show that useful mappings can be learned by preserving distances between different parts of a single sample before and after translation.

Experiments demonstrate one-sided mapping and report preferable numerical results compared with an existing circularity-based constraint. The contribution is a way to guide translation through distance relationships without requiring a separately learned reverse mapping. The results support both the between-sample and within-sample forms of this idea in the settings examined, and the authors make their implementation publicly available.
neurips-2017-one-sided-unsupervised-doma.tldr: Preserving distances between samples or their parts enables unsupervised domain translation without learning a reverse mapping.

paragraphs: Symbolic datasets such as text and graphs often contain hidden hierarchical structure. Embedding methods represent their elements numerically, but many approaches do not explicitly account for that hierarchy. This paper proposes placing symbolic data in hyperbolic space, specifically an n-dimensional Poincaré ball, to learn representations suited to this structure.

The choice of geometry allows the embeddings to capture both hierarchy and similarity in compact representations. These are complementary relationships: an embedding should convey how elements are related within a hierarchy as well as how similar they are. The authors provide an efficient learning algorithm based on Riemannian optimization, which accommodates the geometry of the embedding space.

Experiments show that Poincaré embeddings can substantially outperform Euclidean embeddings on data containing latent hierarchies. The reported advantages concern both representation capacity and generalization ability. The findings therefore support matching the geometry of the representation to hierarchical data, with the demonstrated gains specifically tied to datasets exhibiting that underlying structure.
neurips-2017-poincare-embeddings-for-lea.tldr: Poincaré embeddings use hyperbolic geometry to compactly capture hierarchy and similarity, with substantial gains on hierarchical data.

paragraphs: In a dueling-bandit problem, the learner receives noisy comparisons between two actions. This paper considers actions drawn from a continuous space, with their quality governed by a cost function. The challenge is to use these comparisons to make progressively better decisions while controlling the accumulated cost of learning.

The authors propose a stochastic mirror-descent algorithm and prove a regret bound of order √(T log T). The guarantee assumes that the cost function is strongly convex and smooth. Because this bound grows more slowly than the number of rounds T, the average regret decreases as learning proceeds within the studied setting.

The paper also establishes an equivalence between minimizing dueling-bandit regret and solving the associated convex optimization problem. This connection lets the authors use a convex-optimization lower bound to assess their algorithm. They conclude that it attains an optimal optimization convergence rate and optimal dueling-bandit regret apart from a logarithmic factor, providing a near-optimality result for comparison-based learning under the stated assumptions.
neurips-2017-regret-analysis-for-continu.tldr: Under strong convexity and smoothness, stochastic mirror descent achieves continuous dueling-bandit regret optimal up to a logarithmic factor.

paragraphs: Releasing a sample from a Bayesian posterior produces a randomized output influenced by the underlying data. This paper studies the privacy of releasing one such sample using Rényi differential privacy, or RDP. The analysis asks how posterior sampling can limit the effect that an individual data point has on the released result.

A central ingredient is the prior distribution. The authors exploit its ability to moderate the influence of individual observations, making the prior part of the privacy mechanism. Their focus is sampling in exponential-family settings and specific generalized linear models, including logistic regression. This gives the work a concrete statistical scope.

The paper introduces new RDP mechanisms and supplies an RDP analysis of an existing method. Each method can achieve arbitrary RDP privacy guarantees, and experiments provide evidence of efficacy. The contribution combines mechanism design with privacy accounting, showing how posterior sampling and prior choice can be used within the RDP framework for the model families considered.
neurips-2017-renyi-differential-privacy-.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes Rényi-private posterior-sampling mechanisms that use priors to limit individual observations' influence.

paragraphs: Learning a linear decision boundary with few labeled examples is difficult when labels can be wrong. This paper proposes an efficient Perceptron-based active learner for homogeneous halfspaces, whose boundaries pass through the origin. Its guarantees assume inputs are uniformly distributed over the unit sphere.

Under bounded noise, each label can be flipped with probability at most η, where η is below one-half. The algorithm achieves near-optimal label complexity scaling, up to logarithmic factors, as d log(1/ε)/(1−2η)². Here d is dimension and ε is the target error. The result makes explicit how increasing noise raises the number of labels needed.

The authors also analyze adversarial label corruption under their stated tolerance on the corrupted fraction. In that setting, label complexity is near-optimal and scales as d log(1/ε), up to logarithmic factors. Both settings come with computational runtime guarantees. Finally, the active learner can be converted into an efficient passive learner with near-optimal sample complexity in dimension and target error.
neurips-2017-revisiting-perceptron-effic.tldr: A Perceptron-based learner achieves near-optimal label complexity for noisy homogeneous halfspaces under a uniform spherical input distribution.

paragraphs: This paper introduces self-normalizing neural networks to make deep feed-forward architectures easier to train. Their key component is the scaled exponential linear unit, or SELU, activation function. Its self-normalizing behavior causes activation statistics to move toward zero mean and unit variance as signals pass through layers.

Using the Banach fixed-point theorem, the authors prove convergence for activations starting close to those target statistics, including in the presence of noise and perturbations. They also prove upper and lower variance bounds outside the near-unit-variance case and connect these bounds to avoiding vanishing and exploding gradients. These properties support depth, strong regularization, and robust learning in the proposed framework.

The evaluation covers 121 UCI tasks, drug-discovery benchmarks, and astronomy tasks. SNNs significantly outperform the competing feed-forward methods across the UCI evaluation, outperform all compared methods on Tox21, and establish a new result on an astronomy dataset. Successful SNN architectures are often very deep, supporting the paper's aim of making multiple levels of representation useful in feed-forward networks.
neurips-2017-self-normalizing-neural-net.tldr: SELU activations give feed-forward networks self-normalizing behavior, supported by convergence analysis and strong results across several benchmark collections.

paragraphs: When labels are expensive, linear regression may need to learn from only a subset of available examples. This paper studies how to select that subset so that its solution is unbiased for the solution using every label. The setup uses a full-rank matrix with more columns than rows and samples at least as many columns as there are rows.

The sampling rule assigns probability in proportion to the squared volume spanned by the selected submatrix's rows. Under this volume-sampling rule, the authors construct an unbiased estimator of the full matrix's pseudoinverse from the sampled subset. They also derive a closed-form covariance, providing an exact characterization of the estimator's variability.

For least-squares regression, the subset's fitted weight vector is consequently an unbiased estimator of the full-data optimum. This means agreement on average over sampled subsets, while individual estimates can vary. The authors also derive total-loss bounds and use their results to develop a volume-sampling algorithm faster than the state of the art.
neurips-2017-unbiased-estimates-for-line.tldr: Volume sampling yields unbiased pseudoinverse and least-squares estimates from subsets, together with covariance formulas and loss bounds.

paragraphs: Decision trees and random forests provide information about which input variables matter alongside their predictions. Practitioners commonly use importance measures based on the impurity information produced by these models. This paper examines the theoretical performance of those methods, addressing a gap between their widespread use and their mathematical characterization.

The main contribution is a set of finite-sample performance guarantees in a high-dimensional setting. These guarantees concern behavior with a limited amount of data, rather than only in an unlimited-data limit. They are derived under various modeling assumptions, so the paper's conclusions connect the usefulness of impurity-based importance to the statistical setting in which it is applied.

An extensive collection of simulations provides additional evidence of the methods' effectiveness. The theoretical and empirical components serve complementary purposes: the guarantees characterize performance under assumptions, while the simulations demonstrate behavior in the cases studied. Together, they provide a firmer basis for understanding a feature-importance tool already commonly used with predictive tree models.
neurips-2017-variable-importance-using-d.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample guarantees and simulation evidence for impurity-based variable importance in high-dimensional tree models.

paragraphs: Minimizing training error requires balancing how well a model fits observed data against how reliably that fit carries over to new data. This paper develops a convex surrogate for variance that makes this tradeoff computationally efficient. The approach targets risk minimization and stochastic optimization, balancing approximation and estimation error.

The construction draws on distributionally robust optimization and empirical likelihood. The authors establish finite-sample and asymptotic results describing the resulting estimator, including certificates of optimality. In some scenarios, the method converges faster than empirical risk minimization because it automatically balances bias and variance. The faster-rate claim is therefore tied to particular scenarios.

Experiments on several classification problems support the theoretical motivation. The estimator trades some absolute performance on the training sample against variance and achieves better test performance than standard empirical risk minimization. These findings show how incorporating variability into a convex objective can improve generalization in the evaluated problems while retaining an efficiently optimizable formulation.
neurips-2017-variance-based-regularizati.tldr: A convex variance surrogate efficiently balances fit and variability, with conditional faster-rate guarantees and improved test performance on classification problems.
